source.title: Regularizing and Optimizing LSTM Language Models
source.authors: Stephen Merity; N. Keskar; R. Socher

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Reports a batch-size comparison on language-model held-out perplexity, a different setting from the image-classifier and language-model batch comparisons named in V5. It does not measure the training–test gap directly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that batch sizes of 40–80 performed better than 10–20 for NT-ASGD, but gives no separate numerical results for that comparison. Its optimizer and regularization ablations report perplexity outcomes, but do not test the specific classifier behaviors in the listed versions. Discussion of SGD versus adaptive optimizers cites prior work rather than reporting the paper's own comparison.
record.test_reason: Section 5 reports an own-result batch-size comparison for NT-ASGD LSTM language models: batches of 40–80 performed better than 10–20. This bears on V5 in a different training setting, but does not establish a large-batch penalty or its removal.
record.authors_conclusion: The record is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that recurrent weight-dropping and other regularizers improve LSTM language modeling, that NT-ASGD outperforms their tested SGD alternative, and that adding a neural cache further improves PTB and WikiText-2 perplexity. They anticipate applicability to other sequence tasks but do not demonstrate it.
record.recipe_differences: Three-layer LSTM language modeling with NT-ASGD, regularization ablations, and held-out perplexity; no random-label memorization or training–test-gap measurement.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors state that batch sizes of 40–80 performed better than 10–20 for NT-ASGD. Their ablation results also show held-out perplexity changes when regularization and optimization components are removed.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing embedding dropout increases test perplexity from 57.3 to 62.7 on PTB and from 65.8 to 68.1 on WT2; removing recurrent weight-dropping increases it to 68.9 and 74.9 respectively (Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Embedding dropout and recurrent DropConnect improve held-out performance in these LSTM language models.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing NT-ASGD with SGD using nonmonotonic learning-rate reductions increases test perplexity from 57.3 to 63.7 on PTB and from 65.8 to 69.7 on WT2 (Section 8, Table 4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Nonmonotonically triggered iterate averaging improves these LSTM language models relative to the tested SGD schedule.

record.problems: The batch-size comparison is reported only as a qualitative statement, with no separate scores or uncertainty. The paper reports perplexity rather than the training–test gap central to the broad claim.
record.rows_left_out: No rows: the batch-size comparison has no separate numerical result, and other quantitative ablations do not measure a behavior named by the tested version.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its comparison with natural-label held-out performance.
Width dependence beyond zero training error.

Own controlled comparisons of adaptive optimizers with SGD, including tuning dependence.

The workload-dependent batch-size threshold, deterioration beyond it, and controlled recovery through recipe changes. The reported batch-size comparison lacks separate scores and an explicit statement that its budgets and other settings were matched; the main recipe uses 750 epochs followed by criterion-stopped fine-tuning.
Dropout effects in fully connected or convolutional classifiers, small-training-set dependence, excessive dropout, and joint removal with weight decay under augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its ranking of generalization gaps.

record.verdict_notes: No V5 label is warranted: better performance at 40–80 than at 10–20 does not contradict a penalty beyond an unspecified workload-dependent threshold, nor establish that adaptation removed such a penalty. Held-out perplexity is an appropriate V5 outcome; an explicit training–test gap is unnecessary. The qualitative batch comparison is already declared in rows_left_out, so it is not listed as missing.
